provenance.notes: B2b family batch, quote archetype override. Licensed low-voltage trade: no camera, panel or monitoring brands, no crime or insurance outcome claims, no privacy-law advice, and the alarm licence stays a placeholder. Ranges are planning figures, not quotes.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Upload a floor plan or photos, mark entrances, parking, registers and blind spots, and say what each camera needs to see, for the site survey
pageStructurePlus.why: Buyers think in areas, not camera counts. A coverage planner turns 'I need cameras' into a scoped security quote.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Self-monitoring versus professional monitoring, what happens when an alarm trips, cellular backup, contract terms as the company sets them, and cancellation
pageStructurePlus.why: Monitoring contracts are where trust is won or lost. Plain terms beat the door-knocker contracts customers have been burned by.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Switching from another alarm or camera provider, which sensors, cameras and wiring can be reused, and what has to be replaced
pageStructurePlus.why: Many buyers already have equipment from a company they're leaving. A takeover page wins them without a full rip-out quote.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Door readers, key fobs and mobile credentials, visitor management, multi-door and multi-site admin, and integration with the alarm and camera system
pageStructurePlus.why: Access control is the business buyer's biggest security ticket. A page for it moves the installer from home alarms to commercial contracts.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Where camera footage is stored, who can view it, retention as the owner chooses, camera signage, and a note to confirm local rules with their own adviser
pageStructurePlus.why: Business owners and landlords ask where recordings go before they sign. Answering plainly removes a quiet objection.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Annual system checks, battery and sensor replacement, camera cleaning and firmware updates, and the response window for service calls
pageStructurePlus.why: Owners worry that the security installer disappears after install. A visible service plan sells the recurring revenue the trade depends on.

openers.line: Your security company's Google listing has no website, so a shop owner who just had a break-in can't see what alarm or camera systems you put in before they call.
openers.hook: Open their Maps listing and confirm there is no Website button. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: What that shop owner could see instead: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your listing goes to a Facebook page with camera install shots and promo posts. A business owner comparing security installers wants monitoring terms and a quote form, not a feed.
openers.hook: Tap the Website link and confirm it lands on Facebook. Note the newest install post.
openers.linkLine: A security site built for the buyer comparing installers: {demo-link}

openers.line: The site on your listing shows a free-host banner and a camera package from years ago. In security, an outdated site makes people wonder if the monitoring is outdated too.
openers.hook: Open the site and note one stale detail: old products, an old year or a dead form.
openers.linkLine: Same security company, current and trustworthy: {demo-link}

openers.line: On my phone your alarm site's quote button sits under a pop-up that won't close. People look for security help on their phone, often right after something happened.
openers.hook: Only if they have a site. Load it on your phone and note what breaks. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: Your security site on a phone: {demo-link}

openers.line: There's no way to request a security site survey except calling. A form that takes a floor plan, entry count and what the cameras need to see would bring in scoped jobs.
openers.hook: Check their site and listing for a survey or quote form with upload. If none, the angle holds.
openers.linkLine: A site survey request with floor plan upload: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your posts of tidy camera runs and labelled rack panels show the craft that separates a good security installer from a cheap one, and they disappear in a week.
openers.hook: Find one clean wiring, rack or camera mount post. Name the job type if they reply.
openers.linkLine: Your install work on a page that stays: {demo-link}

openers.line: A review saying your tech came the same day when an alarm panel kept false-alarming is the line a frustrated customer of another company needs to see.
openers.hook: Read their reviews and copy one phrase about service or response. Quote it if they reply.
openers.linkLine: Your service reviews beside the takeover page: {demo-link}

openers.line: Before the holidays, shop owners and homeowners leaving town start thinking about cameras and alarms. The security installers they find that month get the jobs.
openers.hook: Use in autumn before the holidays, or before a local busy travel season. Name it.
openers.linkLine: A security page ready for the pre-holiday rush: {demo-link}

openers.line: Break-ins get discovered at six in the morning, and the owner calls a security company before opening. If your line goes to voicemail, the camera job goes elsewhere.
openers.hook: Call their number early or late and note whether anything takes the request.
openers.linkLine: A security page that takes the early morning call: {demo-link}

openers.line: Saw you're hiring a low-voltage technician. Good techs check an alarm company online before they apply, and so do the businesses you bid on.
openers.hook: Only if they posted a hiring note or job listing. Note the date.
openers.linkLine: A security company site with a careers page: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your vans install cameras across the county, but nothing online lists the towns you cover. A business owner two towns away assumes you won't come out for a security survey.
openers.hook: Look for posts or reviews from other towns. Name the furthest one.

openers.line: People hesitate on a security system because of upfront cost and long monitoring contracts. A page that explains your payment options and monitoring terms plainly answers it before the call.
openers.hook: Only if they offer monitoring or payment plans. Check posts and listing first. Never state their terms for them.
openers.linkLine: Alarm monitoring and payment options, explained: {demo-link}

openers.line: Business owners ask whether a security installer is licensed for alarm work and insured before they hand over door codes. A page that shows what you hold answers it.
openers.hook: Look for licence or insurance mentions on their listing or vans. Never claim a licence or number you didn't see.
openers.linkLine: Licensing and insurance on one security page: {demo-link}

openers.line: It sounds like a lot of your security work comes through electricians and builders. When they change their low-voltage sub, the work stops unless owners can find you directly.
openers.hook: Look for posts or reviews mentioning builders or electricians. Quote one.
openers.linkLine: Where a direct security buyer would find you: {demo-link}

openers.line: That {specific recent job} you posted is clean security work. An install like that belongs on a page a business owner can look at before booking a survey.
openers.hook: Pick their newest install post and name it: the property type and whether it was cameras, alarm or access control.
openers.linkLine: That install on a security project page: {demo-link}

sequence.dm1:
Hi {Owner} — that {specific recent job} you posted is clean security work.

I looked for a site for {Business Name} and couldn't find anywhere an owner could request a site survey, read your monitoring terms or see your camera installs. I put together a sample security site with a coverage planner and a monitoring plans page, with marked placeholders where your photos would go.

Would it help if I sent it over?
sequence.dm2:
{Owner} — following up in case my last message got buried between installs. Here's the sample security site for {Business Name}: {demo-link}

It has a site survey request with floor plan upload, a plain-language monitoring page, and a takeover page for people leaving another alarm company. If it's not useful, tell me and I'll leave you alone.
sequence.call:
"Hi, is this {Owner}? I'm {Your Name}, I build websites for security and alarm companies here in {City}. I sent you a message a couple of days ago, did it come through?"

IF NO:
"Easy to miss when you're pulling cable. Short version: I built a sample site for {Business Name} with a camera coverage planner, a monitoring plans page and an access control page, with marked placeholders where your photos would go. Can I email you the link?"

IF YES:
"What did you think?"
 → let them talk, don't fill the silence
"The build runs {Build Range}, then {Care Range} a month for hosting and changes. For a security company your size I'd quote about {Build Price}, about one small business camera system."
"Can I walk you through it for ten minutes this week, between surveys?"

CLOSE:
"I'll send a one-page scope and a deposit invoice. We start the day it clears."

objections.objection: We get our work from builders and electricians.
objections.handler: "Keep them. The site is for the business owner who searches after a break-in and the customer leaving a national alarm company, neither of whom knows your builder."

objections.objection: Customers buy cheap cameras online and install them themselves.
objections.handler: "Some do, and they call when the cameras miss the license plate or the app stops working. A takeover and service page catches exactly those people."

objections.objection: I don't want to post prices for security systems.
objections.handler: "You don't have to. The page explains what drives the price, like door count, camera count and monitoring, and the survey request does the rest."

objections.objection: The big national alarm companies spend more than me on ads.
objections.handler: "They do. You win on being local, licensed and reachable. The site says that clearly, with monitoring terms people can actually read."

objections.objection: I'm too busy installing to deal with a website.
objections.handler: "That's why it's built already. I need about twenty minutes and a few of your install photos, and I write the security pages from what you tell me."
"{Build Range}. For you about {Build Price}, because it's a survey request, a monitoring page and an access control page. About one small camera system."

email.subject: Security survey page for {Business Name}

sequence.voicemail: "Hi {Owner}, it's {Your Name}. I build websites for security and alarm companies in {City}, and I made a sample site for {Business Name} with a site survey request. I'll email you the link. {Your Phone}. Thanks."
sequence.takedown:
{Owner} — I'm taking the {Business Name} security demo down on Friday.

Want me to keep it up? One word is fine either way.
sequence.nurture:
Hi {Owner} — shop owners and homeowners around {City} start asking about cameras and alarms before the holidays. Thought of you.

The security site is still here, same price. {demo-link} if you want another look.

bullets: Peg the build to one small business camera system, not to a single doorbell camera.
The survey request and the monitoring page are the core. Price everything else as additions.
Price residential and commercial sections separately; access control and multi-site work sell to a different buyer.
Never write crime, response-time or insurance-discount claims; describe the system and let the owner's insurer speak for itself.
Charge for the takeover page on its own; switching customers are the fastest closes in this trade.
Keep monthly add-ons well below one monitoring contract's annual value.

lineItems.item: Site survey request with floor plan upload
lineItems.description: Max with floor plan and photo upload, entry and camera area checkboxes and a survey calendar.
Max with a mark-up tool on the uploaded plan, coverage goals per area and a summary sent with the request.
Max with a side-by-side of self and professional monitoring, alarm response steps and terms the owner approves.
Max with door reader types, credential options, multi-site admin and a business inquiry form.
Max with a reuse checklist, photo upload of the existing panel and a takeover request.
Max when the page covers a vertical such as retail, offices, warehouses or churches with sample layouts.

whatElseYouSell.name: Install and panel photo session
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "One session shooting clean camera mounts, labelled racks and keypad installs gives the security site proof without showing anyone's floor plan."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 2, at jobs where the owner agrees and nothing sensitive is visible.

whatElseYouSell.name: Google profile upkeep for security installs
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "Weekly posts of camera, alarm and access control installs keep the profile current when someone searches right after a break-in."

whatElseYouSell.name: Business owner outreach for access control
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A short monthly note to offices, clinics and shops nearby about key fob and door reader systems, pointing to the access control page."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 3, once the access control page is live.

whatElseYouSell.name: Van lettering and yard sign artwork
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "The yard sign and window decal on every alarm customer's property is a small billboard. Fresh artwork with the website keeps it working."
whatElseYouSell.when: Right after launch, at the next sign order.

whatElseYouSell.name: Pre-holiday security campaign
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "Before the holidays, a campaign to homes and shops near past installs offering a camera and alarm check-up."

whatElseYouSell.name: Review requests after install
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A week after the system goes live, the customer gets a short review request while the security app is still new and impressive."

whatElseYouSell.name: Takeover offer mailer
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A mailer to neighbourhoods and business parks offering to take over existing alarm systems without a full replacement."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 4, once the takeover page is live.

withoutAI.route: Electricians who sub low-voltage work to them
withoutAI.whoPays: The electrician, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The electrician who brings you in for cameras and alarms on new builds needs a commercial page as much as you did."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Electricians and security installers share every new build.

withoutAI.whoPays: The locksmith, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The locksmith who installs the door hardware for your access control jobs needs a site that takes lockout and rekey calls."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Access control jobs need both trades, so they refer each other constantly.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "The shop owner whose cameras you installed has a website from years ago. You can introduce me while you're on site."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Owners trust the person who just secured their business.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "Property managers ask you for new fobs and door schedules every week. Their tenant request page is usually a dead email address, and you can introduce me to fix it."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Managers trust the vendor who controls who gets into their buildings.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "The builder who has you pre-wire security in every new home has a portfolio site that doesn't show any of it."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Builders trust their low-voltage partner and need better portfolios.

withoutAI.whoPays: The IT provider, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The IT company that set up the network your security cameras run on serves the same businesses and needs a clearer services page."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Camera and network work overlap, and both serve the same small business owners.

withAI.route: Service call intake for the locksmith
withAI.pitchLine: "Callers describe the lockout or the door hardware problem, and the locksmith gets a drafted job with address and urgency before calling back."
withAI.whyItWorks: Built around the access control jobs the security client shares with them.

withAI.route: Visitor sign-in assistant for business clients
withAI.pitchLine: "Visitors sign in on a tablet, the assistant tells the right employee, and the log sits with the access control records."
withAI.whyItWorks: It extends the security client's access control system to the front desk.

withAI.route: Tenant access request assistant for property managers
withAI.pitchLine: "Tenants request a new fob or after-hours door access by text, and the assistant logs it for the manager to approve."
withAI.whyItWorks: Managers field these requests daily, and the security client runs the system.

withAI.route: Low-voltage scope summariser for the builder
withAI.pitchLine: "The builder uploads plans, and the assistant drafts the security, data and AV pre-wire scope for each home for the low-voltage sub."
withAI.whyItWorks: Builders save time and the security client gets clean scopes.

withAI.route: Ticket triage for the IT provider
withAI.pitchLine: "Business clients describe a problem, and the assistant sorts it into network, computer or camera system tickets before a tech calls."
withAI.whyItWorks: Camera issues go to the security partner, the rest stays with IT.

withAI.pitchLine: "After an incident, the owner describes what happened and the assistant drafts a plain incident summary with times, to attach with their exported security footage."
withAI.whyItWorks: Owners struggle with paperwork after a break-in, and the security client already supports them.

softwareAI.name: Missed-call text-back after break-ins
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Someone calls about cameras while you're on a ladder, gets a text asking for the address and what happened, and you call back with a security survey slot."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Day 30. Needs the business number forwarded and wording they approve.

softwareAI.name: Camera and alarm quote builder
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Pick cameras, sensors, keypads and labour from your own price list, and the security quote with monitoring options builds itself."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs their equipment price list, labour rates and monitoring plans.

softwareAI.name: Survey notes to proposal writer
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Talk through the site survey walking out to the van, and a drafted security proposal with camera locations and scope is ready to review."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3, after the quote builder. Needs past proposals. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Monitoring contract e-sign and renewal reminders
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Alarm monitoring agreements get signed on a phone, and the customer gets a friendly note before the term renews."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs their agreement wording, reviewed by their own adviser, and term dates.

softwareAI.name: Customer system records
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every customer's panel, zones, cameras, recorder location and install date in one record, so any tech can service the security system."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs their install records and a tech to fill gaps.

softwareAI.name: Coverage sketch from floor plan
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Upload the customer's floor plan and goals, and it drafts suggested camera positions for the security tech to check on site."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs past plans with the final camera layouts and the tech's review of every draft. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Service ticket portal
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Customers report an offline camera or a beeping alarm keypad, pick a time and see when the tech is coming."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs the customer records and tech schedule.

softwareAI.name: Camera offline alerts to the office
softwareAI.pitchLine: "When a customer's recorder reports a camera offline, the office gets an alert and the customer gets a note that the security company is on it."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs recorders that can send alerts and the customer's permission.

softwareAI.name: After-hours call answering
softwareAI.pitchLine: "It answers the alarm company line at night, separates service problems from new security inquiries, and books the right one."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs their call rules and on-call process. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Access control admin training hub
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Short how-to pages and clips for each business client's door system: add a fob, remove an employee, pull a door report."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5, once access control jobs are steady. Needs screen recordings from their systems.

softwareAI.name: Equipment and job costing tracker
softwareAI.pitchLine: "See which security jobs made money once cameras, cable, labour and return trips are counted."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6. Needs equipment costs and hours per job.

softwareAI.name: Chatbot for camera and monitoring questions
softwareAI.pitchLine: "It answers 'can I see cameras on my phone' and 'what happens if the alarm goes off' from the company's approved security answers, then books a survey."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs approved answers only. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Service plan renewal and battery reminders
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Customers get a reminder when sensor batteries are due and when their alarm service plan renews, with a booking link."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4, with the customer records. Needs install and plan dates.

softwareAI.name: Takeover equipment checker
softwareAI.pitchLine: "A prospect uploads a photo of their old alarm panel or recorder, and it drafts what can likely be reused for the security tech to confirm."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs past takeover jobs and the tech's notes. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Multi-site security dashboard
softwareAI.pitchLine: "A business with several locations sees each site's alarm status, camera health and open service tickets on one screen."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 7, once a multi-site client signs. Needs the customer records and ticket portal.

softwareAI.name: Review reply drafts for security customers
softwareAI.pitchLine: "When a customer posts about their new cameras or a fast alarm repair, a reply that never mentions their address is ready to approve."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2, with review requests. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Bid notice watcher for security contracts
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Schools, towns and housing authorities post camera and access control bids. It flags the ones in the installer's region with walk-through dates."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6. Needs the portals they're registered on. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Technician applicant screener
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Low-voltage applicants answer questions on cable runs, ladders, licensing progress and background checks, and the owner calls the fits."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Whenever they're hiring. Needs must-haves and pay range. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Tech schedule and route board
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Surveys, installs and service calls on one board per tech, with security system notes attached to each stop."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs tech list and job durations.

softwareAI.name: Install checklist and handover pack
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Techs tick through the install checklist, and the customer gets a handover pack with app logins, zone list and how to arm the alarm."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs their install steps and handover documents.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Independent camera and alarm installers quote from scribbled notes. The floor plan survey and quote builder I made for one installer fits them all."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: The first installer paid for it and taught you the survey workflow.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Owners on the distributor's site find a licensed security installer nearby who buys from that distributor."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Distributors want installer loyalty and busy customers.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Members get a survey request, monitoring page and takeover page as part of membership, built on the alarm template."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Associations need tangible benefits; one deal reaches many alarm dealers.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your dealers sell monitoring and need sites that explain it clearly. I build a security dealer site that sends accounts to your centre."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Wholesale monitoring centres grow when their dealers grow.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: School district or campus access control portal
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Staff badge requests, visitor logs and door schedules in one portal across every building, tied to the existing access control system."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Campuses buy security administration tools; the client's install gives you the context.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Agency licence for the security template
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Agencies with an alarm client can skip writing monitoring and takeover pages. Mine are ready to brand."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Agencies sell the client; you sell the security content and forms.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "The security site is live for an installer near {City}. I'll take one alarm company per territory after that."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Exclusivity is the pitch, and installers rarely work outside their area.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Loss prevention managers see every store's camera health, alarm events and service tickets in one view, from the security installer's data."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Chains want one view across stores, and the client's multi-site dashboard proves it.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Gate codes, unit alarms and cameras across facilities, managed from one admin page the security installer maintains."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Storage operators sell security as the product and buy tools that show it.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Owners estimate a camera or alarm system from the sponsoring installer's own prices and send the survey request directly."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: It never claims market prices, only the sponsor's own.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Rescue of unfinished alarm company apps
routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The alarm company with a stalled project
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "A service portal or quote tool left half-built is a short job. The camera, panel and monitoring logic already runs for another security company."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Budget already committed; they need someone who knows alarm workflows.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Faith communities want cameras, door control and a volunteer safety team page. I build it with the local security installer behind it."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Congregations ask local installers about security, and the client is already the one they trust.

upsellLadder.offer: Security site build plus care plan, one contract
upsellLadder.trigger: They say yes to the demo.
upsellLadder.line: "The security site and the care plan go on one contract, so new camera or alarm pages are a message to me."

upsellLadder.offer: Review requests and Google profile upkeep
upsellLadder.trigger: A customer thanks them for a fast install or alarm repair.
upsellLadder.line: "That thank-you after the alarm repair is the review the next security search needs to see."

upsellLadder.trigger: Survey requests pile up and quotes go out days late.
upsellLadder.line: "Your surveys are waiting on quotes. Build them from your price list the same afternoon."

upsellLadder.offer: Monitoring contract e-sign and renewal reminders
upsellLadder.trigger: A monitoring customer lapses or a paper agreement goes missing.
upsellLadder.line: "Monitoring is the recurring money. Sign it on a phone and remind before renewal so no alarm account slips."

upsellLadder.offer: Business owner outreach for access control
upsellLadder.trigger: The first access control job is finished and photographed.
upsellLadder.line: "You've done one door system. Let's show every office nearby what key fob access looks like."

upsellLadder.trigger: Service calls start crowding out new installs on the schedule.
upsellLadder.line: "Let customers log their own security service tickets and pick a time, and the phone calms down."

upsellLadder.trigger: A business with several locations signs on.
upsellLadder.line: "Give that multi-site client one security screen for every location and the account stays yours."
